clue.text: He might' give one socks in the East End.

definitions.text: He might' give one socks in the East End.

parts.words: He might' give one socks in the East End.
parts.note: a seller of socks and stockings, said with the dropped H of Cockney speech, becomes the word for a willow

explanation.surface: A Cockney shopkeeper hands a customer a pair of socks, or perhaps a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: A hosier sells socks; in the East End of London, where Cockneys drop their H's, he is an 'osier. 'Give one socks' also hints at giving someone a beating.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cockney pronunciation of a hosiery seller's trade name matches the willow used for basket-making.

clue.text: Close enough to be, could one say,

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Close enough to be, could one say, (9)' appears cut short after the final comma: the words that would give the sound-alike wordplay are missing, and there is no scan.
annotationWithheld.clue: Close enough to be, could one say,

clue.text: A deceptive process — as the model said.

definitions.meaning: practising deception on someone, putting one over on them
an artist's model, asked what she was doing

explanation.walkthrough: To impose on someone is to deceive or take advantage of them; the second reading splits the word into I'M POSING.
explanation.definitionFit: Imposition is an old word for trickery, so the act of tricking someone is this gerund.

clue.text: No dual arrangement to get rid of.

indicators.note: an arrangement of the letters puts them in a new order, so these two words are reworked

explanation.surface: Refusing a twin setup is the way to clear things out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' signals the anagram of NODUAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Discharging a load, or dumping something unwanted, is a synonym of disposing of it.

clue.text: Old Prime Minister's point.

definitions.meaning: Lord Frederick ... led the British government from 1770 to 1782, during the American War of Independence
one of the four cardinal points of the compass

explanation.walkthrough: Lord North was the British Prime Minister who lost the American colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardinal compass direction shares its name with the eighteenth-century Tory statesman.

clue.text: There's undoubtedly something in it.

parts.note: the idiom for a claim that has some truth read literally as describing matter itself, the stuff that fills things

explanation.walkthrough: 'There's something in it' usually means an idea has merit; read literally, matter or solid content is what is in anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Solid matter or real content is literally 'something' that occupies a thing.

clue.text: This is getting worse and worse!

definitions.text: This is getting worse and worse!

parts.words: This is getting worse and worse!
parts.note: the exclamation of someone exasperated, read as a plain description of a process of decline

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a complaint but is simply a definition of decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A steady decline in condition or quality is the process of things becoming progressively poorer.

clue.text: Legal right, conferred, it seems, by old helps to understanding.

parts.note: something very old is ancient
lights are aids to knowledge, as in 'according to his lights' or shedding light on a matter

explanation.surface: A legal entitlement seems to be granted by old aids to comprehension.
explanation.walkthrough: In English law a householder who has had daylight through a window for twenty years can stop a neighbour building to block it; such windows bear this name, sometimes on a sign.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the English property-law entitlement to keep receiving daylight through long-established windows.

clue.text: Anyhow Mrs. Proudie lived up designation!

definitions.text: Anyhow Mrs. Proudie lived up designation!

parts.words: Anyhow Mrs. Proudie lived up designation!
parts.note: Mrs Proudie in Trollope's Barchester Towers is the bishop's domineering wife, who behaved as though she held his office herself

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Proudie, the bishop's wife in Trollope's Barchester novels, ran the diocese herself, so she lived up to the title belonging to bishops.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for anything belonging to bishops suits the overbearing wife who acted as one.

clue.text: The bird to display charm in the Navy?

indicators.note: the charm word sits within the letters for the navy

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
obi, or obeah, is a West Indian fetish or charm

explanation.surface: A seabird wonders whether it can show off a lucky amulet while serving with the fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: OBI is an old word for a sorcerer's charm or fetish, from West Indian obeah.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-breasted garden songbird is a familiar British bird.

clue.text: Just the place for lofty brooding.

definitions.text: Just the place for lofty brooding.

parts.words: Just the place for lofty brooding.
parts.note: brooding is not gloomy thought high up but a bird sitting on eggs in a nest set high on a crag

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brooding' suggests moody contemplation; here it is a bird of prey sitting on its eggs, high up.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle's nest built high on a cliff is where such birds incubate their young.

clue.text: A succulent dish possibly the pig's at.

indicators.note: what the letters might possibly become once shuffled, so they are reworked

explanation.surface: A pig is eating something tasty at the trough, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals the anagram of THEPIGSAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin Italian pasta strands are served as a dish.

clue.text: "Shy traffickers, the dark —— co" (M. Arnold.)

parts.note: a line from Matthew Arnold's poem The Scholar-Gipsy, ending 'come', with the people of Spain and Portugal missing

explanation.walkthrough: The closing lines of Arnold's The Scholar-Gipsy describe Tyrian traders meeting the dark people of the Spanish peninsula; the 'co' is the start of 'come', cut short in the printing.
explanation.definitionFit: The inhabitants of ancient Spain and Portugal are named after their peninsula.

clue.text: One way of making our hip be a spurge.

indicators.note: the letters can be made into the plant's name by being rearranged, one way among many

explanation.surface: A gardener muses on how to turn their own hip into a weed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One way of making' signals the anagram of OURHIPBEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurges are the plants of the botanical genus named after an ancient physician, Euphorbus.

clue.text: One (or more) of the big guns.

definitions.text: One (or more) of the big guns.

parts.words: One (or more) of the big guns.
parts.note: the word for a large artillery piece keeps the same form in the plural, hence one or more

explanation.walkthrough: 'Big guns' sounds like important people, but these are actual artillery; the word is the same singular or plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy artillery piece, and the plural of it, share one form.

clue.text: Hitting the mean like this is quite fair.

definitions.text: Hitting the mean like this is quite fair.

parts.words: Hitting the mean like this is quite fair.
parts.note: working out the middle value of a set of figures, where 'quite fair' means middling, just as ordinary as the mean

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite fair' means middling, neither good nor bad, which is what the mean value is; 'hitting the mean' is calculating it.
explanation.definitionFit: Calculating the arithmetic mean of figures is this activity, which yields a middling result.

clue.text: It takes a saint to stimulate this fish.

parts.note: ST is the usual abbreviation for saint
to urge on is to spur or stimulate

explanation.surface: Only a holy man could get this fish moving.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bony fish prized for its roe as caviar.

clue.text: But one Jack of this style was not admirable.

definitions.text: But one Jack of this style was not admirable.

parts.words: But one Jack of this style was not admirable.
parts.note: the old slang word for a splendid fellow is also the surname of the Victorian Whitechapel murderer

explanation.walkthrough: In old British slang a first-rate thing or person was called by this word; the notorious Victorian murderer Jack the Ripper was hardly first-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for an excellent person or thing, also the nickname of the Whitechapel killer.

clue.text: No 7 down in this, it's heavenly.

definitions.text: No 7 down in this, it's heavenly.

parts.words: No 7 down in this, it's heavenly.
parts.note: the clue's cross-reference points at another entry meaning solid matter; something with none of it is airy and celestial

explanation.walkthrough: The entry at 7 down means matter or solidity; something with none of it is airy and celestial.
explanation.definitionFit: Light, airy and seemingly not of this world, as if of the heavens.

clue.text: What one must, do when building an organ!

definitions.text: What one must, do when building an organ!

parts.words: What one must, do when building an organ!
parts.note: an order to cease, read as an organ builder fitting the pipe-controlling knobs into the instrument

explanation.walkthrough: An organ's stops are the knobs that bring sets of pipes into play, so its builder must fit them; the phrase is also a curt order to cease.
explanation.definitionFit: The command to cease doing something doubles as fitting stops into an organ.

clue.text: Like that connubial bicycle.

parts.note: the music-hall song Daisy Bell proposes marriage on 'a bicycle built for two'

explanation.walkthrough: The old song Daisy Bell imagines a wedding with 'a bicycle built for two', a tandem with room for a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle with places for a pair of riders, like a tandem.

clue.text: Legal bar always involved in policies to pedestrians.

indicators.note: the letters are permanently caught up within these words, running across them

explanation.surface: A legal ruling forever bound up with street policies for walkers.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across policiES TO Pedestrians.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to bar someone from asserting something contrary to what they earlier said or did.

clue.text: Lag on maybe at length.

indicators.note: these letters might be another word, maybe, once rearranged

explanation.surface: A tardy person straggles behind, perhaps for a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' signals the anagram of LAGON.
explanation.definitionFit: Lengthwise or onward, extending through the full length of something.

clue.text: Overtraining only becomes apparent in fine weather.

indicators.note: good weather means no rain, so the run of letters spelling rain falling is taken away

explanation.surface: Damage from training too hard shows only when the sun is out.
explanation.walkthrough: Without RAINING, the word in the clue shrinks to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Open and plainly visible, not hidden.

clue.text: "The -of the Immortals had his sport with Tess." (Hardy.)

definitions.text: "The -of the Immortals had his sport with Tess." (Hardy.)

parts.words: "The -of the Immortals had his sport with Tess." (Hardy.)
parts.note: the famous closing line of Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles, with the title of the chief god left blank

explanation.walkthrough: The last paragraph of Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles says that the chief of the Immortals had ended his sport with Tess.
explanation.definitionFit: The presiding head of a body, here the chief of the gods in Hardy's phrase.

clue.text: Messrs wilton and Axminster in style?

definitions.text: Messrs wilton and Axminster in style?

parts.words: Messrs wilton and Axminster in style?
parts.note: Wilton and Axminster are kinds of carpet, imagined as gentlemen given a knighthood

explanation.walkthrough: Wilton and Axminster are English carpet towns and carpet types; a 'carpet knight' is an idle stay-at-home soldier, or one knighted at court on the carpet rather than on the battlefield.
explanation.definitionFit: Old term for soldiers who never saw battle, here literally carpets given knightly titles.
